title: Control Theory
subtitle: Feedback, stability, PID, frequency methods and state space, with runnable Python labs and a PID tuner
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on introduction to classical and modern control: feedback and the control problem, modelling with differential equations and Euler simulation, first and second-order responses with damping and overshoot, transfer functions, poles and Routh-Hurwitz stability, PID design with anti-windup, root locus and Bode margins, state-space models with pole placement, controllability and observers, and digital implementation including delay, sampling and feedforward. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, and two interactive labs let you move poles around the s-plane and tune a PID loop live.

chapters.title: Feedback and the control problem
summary: Control theory is the study of making systems behave as we want. A plant (a motor, a room, a rocket) is driven by an input, and we want its output to follow a target called the setpoint.
An open-loop controller sends a fixed command and hopes. A closed-loop (feedback) controller measures the output, forms the error between setpoint and measurement, and corrects it continuously.
Feedback fights disturbances and uncertainty, but a badly designed loop can oscillate or go unstable.

glossary.def: The system being controlled.
The desired value of the output, also called the reference.
The setpoint minus the measured output.
Using the measured output to adjust the input.
An unwanted outside influence on the plant.

keyPoints: Closed loop: sense, compare, act, repeat.
Too much gain can destabilise a loop.

items: ELI5. A thermostat looks at the room, compares it with what you want, and turns the heater on or off. Looking and correcting again and again is called feedback.

A thermostat is the classic example. You set 21 degrees. A sensor reads the room, the controller compares, and the heater switches on if the room is too cold. The heater is the actuator, the room is the plant, and the loop of measuring and correcting is feedback.

Compare an oven timer. It heats for a fixed time and ignores the temperature. That is open loop. It works only if nothing changes: the same oven, the same food, the same door never opened. As soon as a disturbance enters, the result drifts, and the open-loop controller never knows.

In a closed loop the error is the setpoint minus the measurement, written e equals r minus y. The controller turns the error into a command u. If the error is large and positive the command pushes the output up. As the error shrinks, the push shrinks.

Feedback can be too eager. If you push hard when the error is small, the output overshoots, you push back, it overshoots the other way, and the loop oscillates. Everyone has felt this when adjusting a shower tap with a delay. The art of control is to be firm but not reckless.

Designers judge a loop by four things: stability, meaning it settles; accuracy, meaning it ends near the target; speed, meaning how quickly; and robustness, meaning it still works when the plant differs from the model. This course builds the maths and the code to reason about all four.

practice.title: Proportional loop
practice.intro: Simulate a room: temp[k+1] = temp[k] + 0.1 x u[k] - 0.05 x (temp[k] - 10) where the outside temperature is 10 and u = kp x (setpoint - temp[k]), starting from temp[0] = start. Write p_room(start, setpoint, kp, steps) returning the temperatures after each of the steps steps (not including the start), rounded to 2 decimals.
practice.hint: Compute u each step from the current error.
practice.solution:
def p_room(start, setpoint, kp, steps):
    t = float(start)
    out = []
    for k in range(steps):
        u = kp * (setpoint - t)
        t = t + 0.1 * u - 0.05 * (t - 10)
        out.append(round(t, 2))
    return out

chapters.title: Modelling dynamic systems

maps.title: Modelling
links: Time constant | is | Speed of response

summary: To control a system we need a model: equations for how it changes. Most are differential equations such as dx/dt = f(x, u).
A first-order system, like a cooling cup or a charging capacitor, moves toward its final value exponentially. Its time constant tau is the time to cover about 63 percent of the gap.
We can simulate any model on a computer by stepping through time: Euler's method updates x by the rate times a small time step.

glossary.def: The smallest set of numbers that fully describes the system at a moment.
For a first-order system, tau, the time to complete 63.2 percent of a step change.
The value the output settles to.
A simple simulation rule: x_next = x + dt times dx/dt.
Approximating a nonlinear model by a straight-line model near an operating point.

keyPoints: After 3 tau: 95 percent. After 5 tau: 99 percent.
Euler: x[k+1] = x[k] + dt f(x[k], u[k]).

items: ELI5. When you pour hot tea it cools fast at first and slower later. Describing how things change over time is how we get ready to control them.

A cup of coffee cools quickly at first, then more and more slowly toward room temperature. The rate of cooling is proportional to the gap. That one sentence is a differential equation, and its solution is an exponential curve.

The standard first-order model is tau times dy dt plus y equals K times u. K is the steady-state gain: the final output per unit input. Tau is the time constant. After one tau the output has covered 63 percent of the way, after three tau 95 percent, after five tau 99 percent.

A model describes how the state changes. For a car, the state may be position and velocity. For a circuit, it is the voltages across capacitors and currents in inductors. The state is the minimum memory needed to predict the future given the inputs.

Most useful models cannot be solved with pencil and paper, so we simulate. Euler's method takes small steps: new state equals old state plus the time step times the rate of change. It is crude but easy, and with a small step it is good enough for control studies.
Better methods such as Runge-Kutta take more samples per step.

Real systems are nonlinear: friction, saturation, trigonometry. Near an operating point, though, a straight-line approximation works, and linear theory is rich and powerful. This is linearisation, and it is why linear control theory is so widely useful.

practice.title: Euler simulation
practice.intro: Simulate tau dy/dt = K u - y with Euler's method: y[k+1] = y[k] + dt x (K u - y[k]) / tau, starting at y = 0, with constant input u. Write euler1(K, tau, u, dt, steps) returning the list of y after each step, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.solution:
def euler1(K, tau, u, dt, steps):
    y = 0.0
    out = []
    for k in range(steps):
        y = y + dt * (K * u - y) / tau
        out.append(round(y, 3))
    return out

    T = float(T0)
    out = []
    for i in range(steps):
        T = T + dt * (-k * (T - room))
        out.append(round(T, 3))
    return out

chapters.title: Second-order systems: damping and overshoot

maps.title: Second order
links: Critically damped | is | Fastest no overshoot
Settling time | is | Time to stay close

summary: Many systems, such as a mass on a spring, a pendulum or a motor with inertia, behave as second-order systems, described by a natural frequency wn and a damping ratio zeta.
With little damping (zeta below 1) the response overshoots and rings. At zeta equal to 1 it is critically damped. Above 1 it is overdamped and slow.
Specifications such as percent overshoot and settling time translate directly into zeta and wn.

glossary.def: wn, the frequency at which an undamped system would oscillate.
zeta, how strongly oscillations are suppressed.
How far the peak goes beyond the final value, as a percentage of it.
The time after which the response stays within a small band, often 2 percent, of the final value.
The time to go from 10 percent to 90 percent of the final value.

keyPoints: y'' + 2 zeta wn y' + wn^2 y = wn^2 u.
Poles: -zeta wn plus or minus i wn sqrt(1 - zeta^2).

items: ELI5. A bouncy car with weak shock absorbers keeps wobbling. A stiff one does not wobble but feels hard. The best has just enough squish.

Picture a car's suspension. A worn shock absorber lets the car bounce many times after a bump. A good one lets it settle in one smooth motion. A stiff one makes it feel sluggish. These three cases are underdamped, near critically damped, and overdamped.

The standard form has two numbers. The natural frequency wn says how fast things want to move. The damping ratio zeta says how much friction fights the oscillation. Zeta of zero never stops ringing, zeta of one is the fastest response without overshoot, and larger values are slower and smoother.

For a step input the underdamped response overshoots the target by a predictable amount: exp of minus pi zeta over the square root of one minus zeta squared. At zeta of 0.5 that is about 16 percent. At 0.7 it is about 5 percent, a popular design target.

The settling time to within two percent is roughly four divided by zeta times wn. The product zeta wn is the decay rate, set by the real part of the poles. So the shape of the response is read from where the poles are: far left means fast decay, high up means fast ringing.

These formulas let designers work backwards. If the specification says less than ten percent overshoot and settle in two seconds, we compute the needed zeta and wn, and then choose controller gains that place the closed-loop poles accordingly. The poles lab lets you see the connection yourself.

practice.title: Simulate a second-order step
practice.intro: Euler-simulate y'' = wn^2 (u - y) - 2 zeta wn y' with u = 1 and zero start. Use v = y' : v += dt x acceleration, then y += dt x v (update v first). Write sim2(zeta, wn, dt, steps) returning y after each step, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Update the velocity, then the position.
practice.solution:
def sim2(zeta, wn, dt, steps):
    y = 0.0
    v = 0.0
    out = []
    for k in range(steps):
        a = wn * wn * (1.0 - y) - 2 * zeta * wn * v
        v = v + dt * a
        y = y + dt * v
        out.append(round(y, 3))
    return out

chapters.title: Transfer functions and stability

maps.title: Stability
links: Laplace transform | turns | Calculus into algebra
Transfer function | is | Output over input
Stable | means | Poles in left half-plane
Final value | is | Gain at s = 0

summary: The Laplace transform replaces differentiation by multiplication by s. A linear system then becomes a transfer function G(s) = Y(s) / U(s), a ratio of polynomials in s.
The roots of the denominator are the poles. A continuous-time system is stable when all poles have negative real parts, lying in the left half of the s-plane.
Routh-Hurwitz checks stability from the coefficients alone, without finding the roots. Closing a loop changes the poles, which is how feedback reshapes behaviour.

glossary.def: G(s) = Y(s) / U(s), the ratio of output to input in the Laplace domain.
The region of the s-plane where the real part is negative; poles there mean decay.
The denominator of the closed-loop transfer function set to zero; its roots are the closed-loop poles.
A table test of stability using only polynomial coefficients.
A steady-state output equals G(0) times the input for a stable system and a unit step.

keyPoints: Stable iff all poles have Re < 0.
Second order: stable iff all coefficients positive.

items: ELI5. Every machine has hidden numbers called poles. If they are on the good side, wobbles die away. If they are on the bad side, wobbles grow and grow.

The Laplace transform is a trick. Differentiation in time becomes multiplication by s, so differential equations become polynomials. A transfer function G of s is the output over the input for a system starting at rest. It captures everything about a linear time-invariant system.

A pole is a value of s where G blows up, a root of the denominator. A pole at minus two gives a decaying exponential e to the minus two t. A pole at plus two gives a growing one, e to the plus two t, so the system is unstable.
Complex pole pairs give oscillations whose envelope decays when the real part is negative.

So stability has a clear picture: draw the s-plane and put a cross at each pole. All crosses in the left half means the system is stable. Any cross in the right half means it is unstable. Crosses on the imaginary axis give sustained oscillation, which is marginal stability.

Feedback changes the poles. With a controller C and plant P, the loop transfer function is L equals C times P, and the closed loop is L over one plus L. The closed-loop poles solve one plus L equals zero. Raising a gain moves the poles; the root locus is the picture of their paths.

Finding roots of a high-order polynomial is hard by hand, so Routh and Hurwitz found a way to tell whether any root lies in the right half-plane directly from the coefficients. For a second-order polynomial the rule is easy: all coefficients must be positive.
For third order, a2 a1 must exceed a3 a0 as well.

chapters.title: PID control
summary: The PID controller computes its command from three terms: proportional to the error now, integral of the error so far, and derivative of the error's rate of change.
Proportional control alone often leaves a steady-state error. The integral term removes it by acting until the error is exactly zero. The derivative term damps oscillation by reacting to the trend.
Practical PID needs care: limit the output, stop the integrator winding up when saturated, and filter the derivative to avoid amplifying noise.

glossary.def: Kp times the current error.
Ki times the accumulated error over time; removes steady-state error.
Kd times the rate of change of the error; adds damping.
Excessive growth of the integral term while the actuator is saturated.
The remaining error after transients have died.

keyPoints: u = Kp e + Ki integral(e) + Kd de/dt.
Discrete: I += e dt; D = (e - e_prev) / dt.
Raise Ki: removes offset, more oscillation.

items: ELI5. A PID controller is like a careful driver. One part steers by how far off you are, one by how long you have been off, and one by how fast you are moving.

About nine out of ten industrial control loops use PID. Cruise control, drone stabilisers, ovens and chemical plants all run it. It is popular because three intuitive knobs often suffice and it needs only a rough idea of the plant.

Think of steering a car toward a lane centre. The proportional term is steering in proportion to how far off you are. The integral term is the gentle persistent nudge that cancels a steady crosswind you have noticed has been pushing you for a while.
The derivative term is easing off because you are already closing in fast.

Proportional alone leaves an offset when the plant needs a constant effort to hold the target, since zero error would mean zero push. The integral term keeps growing while any error persists, so it finally supplies exactly the effort required and the error vanishes.

Too much integral causes slow oscillations. Too much proportional causes fast oscillation. The derivative term helps by opposing rapid motion, but because it differentiates, it magnifies measurement noise, so real controllers filter it. A tuner explores these trade-offs.

Two practical fixes matter. First, the actuator has limits; a heater cannot go below off. If the integrator keeps accumulating while saturated, it takes a long time to unwind afterwards. Anti-windup stops it from accumulating then.
Second, derivative kick: use the derivative of the measurement, not the error, so a setpoint jump does not cause a spike.

practice.title: PID output
practice.intro: Write pid_step(e, e_prev, integral, kp, ki, kd, dt): one PID step. New integral = integral + e x dt; derivative = (e - e_prev) / dt. Return the list [u, new_integral] with u = kp e + ki new_integral + kd derivative, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
def pid_step(e, e_prev, integral, kp, ki, kd, dt):
    integral = integral + e * dt
    d = (e - e_prev) / dt
    u = kp * e + ki * integral + kd * d
    return [round(u, 4), round(integral, 4)]

practice.title: Closed-loop PI simulation
practice.intro: Plant: y[k+1] = y[k] + dt x (u - y[k]). Controller PI with output u = kp e + ki I where e = r - y, and I += e dt before computing u. Start y = 0, I = 0. Write pi_sim(r, kp, ki, dt, steps) returning y after each step, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Compute e, integrate, then drive the plant.
practice.solution:
def pi_sim(r, kp, ki, dt, steps):
    y = 0.0
    integ = 0.0
    out = []
    for k in range(steps):
        e = r - y
        integ = integ + e * dt
        u = kp * e + ki * integ
        y = y + dt * (u - y)
        out.append(round(y, 3))
    return out

chapters.title: Root locus and frequency response

maps.title: Frequency methods
links: Bode plot | shows | Gain and phase

summary: Root locus shows how the closed-loop poles move as a gain k grows from zero to infinity, giving a picture of when the loop becomes unstable.
Frequency response describes how a system treats sine inputs. A Bode plot draws gain and phase against frequency. Margins measure how close the loop is to instability.
Gain margin and phase margin are safety distances. A phase margin of 45 to 60 degrees usually means a well-damped loop.

glossary.def: The set of closed-loop pole positions as a gain varies.
A graph of a system's gain (in decibels) and phase against frequency.
The frequency where the loop gain magnitude equals 1 (0 dB).
How much extra phase lag at gain crossover would make the loop marginally stable.
How much the gain could rise before instability, measured where the phase is minus 180 degrees.

items: ELI5. Before a boat is built, you can test it on paper by asking how it answers slow waves and fast waves. Frequency tests show how close it is to going out of control.

Push a child on a swing. Pushes in time with the swing build it up; pushes against it cancel. Systems respond to sine inputs in a similar way: each frequency is amplified or reduced, and delayed by some amount. That is the frequency response.

For a transfer function G of s, put s equal to i w and you get the gain and phase at frequency w. A Bode plot draws the gain in decibels, twenty times the log of the magnitude, and the phase in degrees, both against frequency on a logarithmic axis.
Simple systems give straight-line asymptotes that are easy to sketch.

Why care? Because a loop goes unstable when, at the frequency where the loop is turned around by 180 degrees, the gain is still one or more. Feedback then turns negative into positive and reinforces itself. The margins measure how far from that state you are.

Phase margin is the extra delay the loop can tolerate at the crossover frequency. Gain margin is how many times the gain could be multiplied. Rules of thumb: phase margin above 45 degrees and gain margin above 2, which is 6 decibels.
These numbers protect against the plant being a little different from the model.

Root locus complements this view. Plot the poles as gain k rises. Branches start at the open-loop poles and head toward the zeros or to infinity. If a branch crosses into the right half-plane at some k, that k is the stability limit. Together, Bode and root locus are the classical design toolbox.

chapters.title: State space and state feedback

maps.title: State space
links: Controllability | asks | Can inputs steer all states
Observability | asks | Can outputs reveal states

summary: State-space models write a system as x' = A x + B u and y = C x, handling many inputs and outputs and giving direct access to internal variables.
State feedback u = -K x changes the closed-loop matrix to A - B K. If the system is controllable, K can place the closed-loop poles anywhere we like.
If we cannot measure all states, an observer estimates them from the outputs. A controller plus an observer is the basis of modern control, including the Kalman filter.

glossary.def: x' = A x + B u, y = C x, a first-order matrix description of a linear system.
Whether the input can move the state to any desired value.
Whether the state can be deduced from the outputs.
Choosing the feedback gain K so that A - B K has chosen eigenvalues.
A model-based estimator of the internal state from inputs and outputs.

keyPoints: u = -K x gives x' = (A - B K) x.
Controllable if [B, AB, ...] has full rank.

items: ELI5. A robot may not be able to see everything it needs, so it keeps a little inner copy of itself to guess the hidden parts.

A mass on a spring has two state variables: position and velocity. Once you know both, you can predict the future given the forces. State space writes the equations of motion as one matrix equation, x dot equals A x plus B u, where x is a list of the state variables.

The A matrix says how the state drifts by itself and the B matrix says how the input pushes it. The eigenvalues of A are the poles. A system with an eigenvalue in the right half-plane is unstable, however its equations are dressed up.

State feedback uses all the state variables: u equals minus K x. Then x dot equals A minus B K, times x. We choose K to move the poles where we want, for example to give a damping ratio of 0.7 and a chosen speed.
This is pole placement, and for a second-order system the arithmetic is a simple matching of coefficients.

Can you always do this? Only if the system is controllable: the input must be able to reach every state. The test builds the matrix with columns B, A B, A squared B and so on, and checks its rank. Likewise, observability asks whether the outputs reveal the state.
When a state cannot be measured, an observer runs a copy of the model alongside the plant and corrects it using the measured output. The Kalman filter does so optimally when noise is Gaussian.
Combine an observer and state feedback and you have an output-feedback controller, widely used in aircraft, spacecraft and robots.

practice.title: Controllable 2x2?
practice.intro: For x' = A x + B u with 2 states, the system is controllable when the determinant of [B, A B] is non-zero. Write controllable(A, B): True or False, where B is a list of 2 numbers.
practice.hint: Form the 2x2 matrix from B and AB.
practice.solution:
def controllable(A, B):
    ab0 = A[0][0] * B[0] + A[0][1] * B[1]
    ab1 = A[1][0] * B[0] + A[1][1] * B[1]
    det = B[0] * ab1 - B[1] * ab0
    return abs(det) > 1e-9

chapters.title: Digital control and practical design
summary: Controllers run on computers at a fixed sample time T. A zero-order hold keeps each command constant between samples. The model and the PID must be discretised.
Sampling and computation add delay, which eats phase margin, so a good rule is to sample 10 to 20 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth.
Real designs deal with actuator limits, sensor noise, dead zones, delays and modelling errors. Robustness means still working when the plant is not exactly as modelled.

glossary.def: The period T between controller updates.
Holding the controller output constant between samples.
A pure delay between input and output effects.
Ability to keep performance despite model error and disturbances.
Adding a command based on the known setpoint or disturbance instead of waiting for error.

keyPoints: Sample 10 to 20 times faster than bandwidth.
Delay costs phase: w T radians.

items: ELI5. A computer controller looks at the world many times a second. If it looks too slowly or its message is late, it can steer badly, so engineers test it on pretend bumps first.

A modern controller is a few lines of code running in a loop. Read the sensor, compute the command, write the actuator, wait for the next tick. The tick period matters. Too slow and the loop cannot respond to changes in time. Too fast wastes computing and amplifies noise in the derivative.

Every delay costs phase. A delay of D seconds adds minus w D radians of phase at frequency w. At the crossover frequency this can cut the phase margin sharply, even push a stable loop into instability. That is why a long dead time, as in a long pipe or a network link, makes control hard.

The discrete PID is simple. The integral becomes a running sum times T, the derivative a difference over T. Add output limits and anti-windup. Filtering the measurement slightly keeps noise from turning into jitter in the command. Use fixed-size arithmetic with care.

Feedback reacts only after an error appears. If you know in advance what is coming, such as a setpoint change or a measurable disturbance, you can add a feedforward term that acts at once, and let feedback clean up the small remainder. Together they give fast, accurate control.
Finally, test the design against reality: change the plant gain by plus or minus thirty percent, add noise, add delay, saturate the actuator. A controller that survives is robust.
Advanced methods such as model predictive control optimise the plan over a horizon within the constraints, and are now common in industry, though PID remains the workhorse.

practice.title: Feedforward plus feedback
practice.intro: Plant: y[k+1] = y[k] + 0.2 (u[k] - y[k]). Command u = ff + kp (r - y) where ff = r (the feedforward guess for a plant of gain 1). Write ff_sim(r, kp, steps, start): y after each step starting at y = start, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Add the feedforward and the feedback parts.
practice.solution:
def ff_sim(r, kp, steps, start):
    y = float(start)
    out = []
    for k in range(steps):
        u = r + kp * (r - y)
        y = y + 0.2 * (u - y)
        out.append(round(y, 4))
    return out
